chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam, from Sadeer al-Sayrafi, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'What prevents you from freeing a person every day?' I said, 'My wealth cannot bear that.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Feeding a Muslim every day?' So I said, 'The rich or the poor?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'For the rich may also desire food.'

key_terms.نَسَمَة: A person/soul (often used for freeing a slave)

ai.seo_question: What is the recommended daily act of charity if one cannot afford to free a slave?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) offers a practical alternative to manumission, emphasizing that feeding a Muslim is a continuous act of charity (sadaqah) that yields daily reward. The Imam’s clarification that the wealthy are included—despite their ability to afford food—highlights the Shia scholarly understanding that the spiritual benefit lies in the consistency of the act and the intention of giving, rather than merely alleviating the recipient's hunger. This underscores the importance of regular, sustained charity over sporadic, large-scale gestures.
